props.title: Wag the Dog

sections.content: Wag the Dog landed like a prophetic bombshell, releasing just weeks before the Clinton-Lewinsky scandal. David Mamet's razor-sharp screenplay follows a spin doctor (Robert De Niro) and Hollywood producer (Dustin Hoffman) manufacturing a fake war to distract from a presidential scandal. The film's cynical take on media manipulation feels more relevant than ever in our era of "fake news" and viral disinformation. Hoffman's character, reportedly based on producer Robert Evans, delivers a masterclass in how entertainment industry techniques can shape political narratives.

sections.content: The film kicked off a wave of political media satires that peaked in the late 90s and early 2000s. The Truman Show (1998) examined reality TV's manipulation of truth, while Bulworth (1998) skewered political messaging and campaign finance. These films reflected growing public awareness of how media shapes political narratives. Thank You for Smoking (2005) later continued this tradition, focusing on a tobacco lobbyist's expert spin techniques.

Director Barry Levinson's documentary background adds crucial authenticity to Wag the Dog's newsreel footage and media manipulation scenes. The film shares DNA with earlier political paranoia thrillers like The Parallax View (1974) and Three Days of the Condor (1975), but shifts focus from conspiracy to media construction of reality. Its influence extends to modern series like House of Cards (2013-2018) and films like Vice (2018). SUBHEAD: Media Manipulation in Modern Cinema

sections.content: Recent films continue exploring themes Wag the Dog pioneered. Nightcrawler (2014) examines how news footage can be staged and manipulated, while The Post (2017) shows journalism's role in exposing government deception. Don't Look Up (2021) updates media manipulation themes for the social media age, showing how even existential threats can be spun and distorted for political gain.
